rationale: A scan of this app's whole BSB text finds the phrase 'the garden of the LORD' exactly twice: Genesis 13:10, where Lot sees the Jordan plain 'well watered like the garden of the LORD,' and Isaiah 51:3, where the LORD 'will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD' -- one verse after Isaiah 51:2 names Abraham outright ('Look to Abraham your father... When I called him, he was but one'). The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges cross-references each verse to the other (on Genesis 13:10, 'The garden of Jehovah' is the garden of Eden, citing Isaiah 51:3; on Isaiah 51:3, citing Genesis 13:10), and Matthew Poole lists Isaiah 51:3 as 'The like comparison.' The movement runs in opposite directions: in Genesis a garden-like plain is about to be destroyed (13:10's own parenthesis), while in Isaiah a desolation is to be made garden-like. Isaiah 51:3 is not the only later text with this shape: Poole and the Cambridge Bible also cite Ezekiel 28:13 and 31:8 alongside it, and Ezekiel 36:35 (BSB) has the same desolation-to-garden movement, 'This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden,' though with 'Eden' rather than 'the garden of the LORD.' Graded motif because what can be checked is a shared, rare phrase together with Abraham's name in the adjacent verse, and plausible rather than strong because the sources read for this lesson cross-reference the two verses but none argues that Isaiah deliberately recalls Genesis 13:10 rather than the Eden tradition in general; the English count is the BSB's, and the Hebrew was not independently counted.
